title: Function-integrated injectable poly(methyl methacrylate) bone cement engineered with silver-templated mesoporous calcium-silicate nanoparticles  via  a chitosan–glycerophosphate hydrogel
content: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement remains a mainstay of bone reconstruction, yet its high polymerization exotherm, mismatched stiffness, bioinertness and lack of antibacterial activity can lead to thermal injury, stress shielding and post-operative infection. Here we report a single-phase strategy that addresses these limitations together. Mesoporous calcium-silicate nanoparticles (MCSNs) and silver-templated MCSNs (Ag-MCSNs) were dispersed in a thermosensitive chitosan–glycerophosphate (CS–GP) hydrogel and blended with PMMA to prepare three modified cements. The hydrogel phase lowered the peak polymerization temperature from ∼77 °C to below 40 °C, extended the working time beyond 20 min and created interconnected pores throughout the PMMA matrix with a dominant pore diameter of ∼79 µm. The modified cements exhibited an elastic modulus of 140–170 MPa and a compressive yield strength of 7–10 MPa, closely matching cancellous bone, and these properties were retained after 28 days of immersion in simulated body fluid. The MCSN-containing cements additionally promoted apatite deposition, with cumulative calcium uptake reaching 2.8–3.3 mmol L−1 at day 28. Antibacterial testing against E. coli and S. aureus showed that only the Ag-MCSN cement produced clear inhibition zones, disrupted bacterial membranes on contact, and significantly reduced the number of recoverable colonies (p < 0.05) without compromising cytocompatibility. A single Ag-MCSN phase can therefore endow PMMA cement with combined bioactivity and antibacterial activity while improving its thermal and mechanical performance, a combination that holds promise for infection-resistant bone reconstruction.
